reels.title: Who may see this column?

beats.say: Two thousand people query the lake. Who should see a customer's email address?
Access control decides who may read which tables, which columns and which rows. The goal is the least access each person needs, granted quickly.
Most people need the table but not the personal values. So the default is: see the rows, with personal columns masked.
Good access control says yes quickly to most things, and no clearly to a few.

check.q: What is a safe default for an analyst reading a customer table?
opts: See the rows with personal columns masked
See nothing until a committee meets
See every column in full by default
check.why: Most work needs the table, not the personal values.

work: List the tables in your lake with personal data.
Write who needs the full values, and why.

reels.title: Roles or attributes

beats.say: Why do some companies end up with thousands of roles?
Role-based access gives permissions to roles. But one role per team, dataset and sensitivity multiplies until nobody knows what any role allows.
Attribute-based access decides from attributes: the user's team and purpose, the data's tags. A few policies cover thousands of cases.

show.title: Attribute policies
items: PII masked unless purpose is support

beats.say: Use both: coarse roles for which domains you may query, and tags with attributes for the fine rules.

check.q: Why does attribute-based access scale better for fine rules?
opts: A few policies on tags replace many roles
It removes the need for any policies
It gives everyone full access by default
check.why: Attributes of users and data combine into a handful of policies.

work: Count the roles in your warehouse.
Write one tag policy that could replace ten of them.

reels.title: Rows, columns and expiry

beats.say: Column rules, row rules, and access that never ends.
Column rules mask or deny values. Row rules filter which records a user sees, for example only their own region.
Rare access should be just in time: granted for a day, then removed. And every quarter, owners review who still has access and remove what nobody can justify.
Enforce the same rules in every engine that reads the lake, or people will use the one without rules.

check.q: Why must rules be enforced in every engine that reads the lake?
opts: People will use the engine without rules
Engines are faster with more rules
Auditors only check one engine
check.why: One unprotected engine bypasses all the others.

work: List every engine that reads your lake.
Check which of them enforce your masking rules.

reels.title: Designing access for a staff interview

beats.say: Interview question: design access for a lakehouse with two thousand users.
Roles stay coarse, through a workflow with an owner's approval and an expiry. Fine rules come from tags and attributes.
Enforce at read time in every engine from one policy definition, log every decision for audit, and review grants every quarter.
Measure it: time to get access, roles in use, expired grants removed, and columns with a reviewed tag.

check.q: Which number shows access control is not slowing people down?
opts: Time from request to granted access
Number of roles in the warehouse
Number of policies in the catalog
check.why: Fast, safe access is the goal; time to access measures the first half.

work: Measure time to access last month.
Write the four numbers you would report.

reels.title: Governance in one minute

beats.say: Governance sounds like a committee that says no. It should be the opposite.
Governance is how people use data quickly without fear: knowing what exists, who may see it, protecting personal data by default, and proving it.

show.title: Its jobs
items: Keep it only as long as allowed

beats.say: The test: a new analyst gets access in hours, never sees a raw card number, and you can say who read a customer's data last month in minutes.
All of it works only when it lives in the platform as code, not in documents.

check.q: What is the test of good governance?
opts: Fast, safe access and answers in minutes
The number of review meetings held
How many documents describe the rules
check.why: Governance should speed safe use and prove it quickly.

work: Time how long a new analyst waits for access.
Try to answer who read one customer's data last month.

reels.title: Finding personal data

beats.say: You cannot protect what you have not found.
Tags come from three places: teams declare them in contracts, a scanner detects them from sample values, and owners review what the scanner proposes.
A scanner tags a column only when most values match a pattern, like eighty percent. One email in a notes column does not make it an email column.
Report classification coverage: the share of columns with a reviewed tag.

check.q: Why does a scanner use a threshold before tagging a column?
opts: One stray value should not tag a column
Thresholds make the scanner much slower
Tags must never be proposed by tools
check.why: Most values must match, so free text with one address is not tagged.

work: Scan one raw table for emails and phone numbers.
Send the proposed tags to the owner.

reels.title: Mask, tokenise or pseudonymise

beats.say: Three ways to hide personal data, often mixed up.
Masking hides values at read time; the data is unchanged. Tokenisation swaps values for random tokens a vault can map back. Pseudonymisation uses a keyed hash so joins still work.
A plain hash of an email is not anonymous: anyone can hash a list of emails and match them. Use a key, and protect it.
Pseudonymised data is still personal data. Only properly anonymised data is not.

check.q: Analysts must join by customer without knowing who they are. What fits?
opts: A keyed hash of the customer id
A plain hash of each email address
Deleting the customer id everywhere
check.why: A keyed hash keeps joins working and cannot be reversed by guessing.

work: Find any plain hashes of emails in your data.
Decide which columns need masking, tokens or keyed hashes.

reels.title: Lineage for governance

beats.say: Lineage is more than a nice graph.
Lineage shows which jobs read which tables and write which others. A personal data tag on a source flows to every derived table, until a step masks or aggregates it.
It also gives impact before a change, root cause after an incident, and every table that holds a person's id for erasure.
Collect it from job runs with OpenLineage, not by parsing SQL afterwards.

check.q: Where should a PII tag stop propagating through lineage?
opts: At a step that masks or aggregates it
At the first table in another domain
Never; every downstream table is PII
check.why: Masking or aggregation removes the personal values, so the tag stops there.

work: Trace one PII column through your lineage.
Mark the steps where it is masked.

reels.title: Erasure in a lakehouse

beats.say: A customer asks to be forgotten. You run the delete. Are they really gone from every table, snapshot and backup?
Find every table with their id from tags and lineage. Delete by id in a weekly batch, with merge-on-read deletes or deletion vectors.
Then compact and expire old snapshots, or time travel still shows the rows. Backups and extracts follow the same rules.
Check legal holds first, and keep evidence: tables touched, rows deleted, snapshots expired.

check.q: After a delete, why can a person's rows still be read in Iceberg?
opts: Old snapshots still point to the old files
Iceberg cannot delete individual rows
Deletes apply only after a rename
check.why: Snapshot expiry and compaction must follow the delete.

work: Run an erasure on a test subject end to end.
Check snapshot expiry runs after it.

reels.title: Retention and legal holds

beats.say: Keeping data forever is not safe. It is a cost and a risk.
Each class of data has a retention period: raw events thirteen months, financial records seven years, chat two years. Jobs delete what has expired.
A legal hold overrides retention. Data in litigation must be kept even past its date, so the deletion job checks holds first.
And never delete data with no rule: list it, and give it a class.

check.q: Retention says delete, but the dataset is under legal hold. What happens?
opts: It is kept and reported until the hold lifts
It is deleted because retention came first
Half of it is deleted to be on the safe side
check.why: Destroying held data is far worse than keeping data too long.

work: Write retention classes for your main datasets.
Check your deletion job reads legal holds first.

reels.title: The auditors are coming

beats.say: External auditors arrive in six weeks, and today access to customer data is granted by chat messages. What do you do first?
Turn on access logs everywhere. Tag and mask the most-read customer tables. Move access to a workflow with approvals and expiry.
Run an access review that removes unjustified grants, and run erasure end to end on a test subject with evidence.
Say plainly what will not be finished, with dates. Auditors trust honest plans.

check.q: What do auditors want to see about customer data access?
opts: Evidence such as logs, grants and reviews
A slide deck describing the intended rules
A promise that rules will be written soon
check.why: Auditors ask for proof: logs, approvals, reviews and deletion records.

work: Check access logging is on in every engine.
List the evidence you could show an auditor today.

reels.title: Who owns governance

beats.say: Who owns data governance in a big company?
A governance lead with legal and security sets policies. The platform team builds classification, enforcement, lineage, retention jobs and audit logs. Data owners tag, approve and review.
Common failures: committees, role explosion, tags that rot, deletion that leaves snapshots, shadow copies, and grants that never expire.
Scale governance to the risk: a tiny company with one database needs an access list and encryption, not a policy engine.

check.q: Who should approve access to a data product?
opts: Its data owner, through a workflow with expiry
A central board meeting once each month
Whoever answers the chat message first
check.why: Owners know the data; a workflow with expiry keeps it fast and auditable.

work: Name the owner who approves access to each key dataset.
Find grants older than a year.

reels.title: Governance is a library, not a locked door

beats.say: Why does data governance have such a bad name? Because people picture a committee that only ever says no.

show.text: Governance = a committee that says no?
show.sub: Done well, it is the opposite

beats.say: Think of a good library. A catalogue tells you which books exist, what they mean, and who looks after each one. Rare books sit in a reading room, and you get a pass in hours, not weeks. Private letters have names blacked out before you read them.
A sign-in sheet records who read what. Old books are retired on a schedule. So governance is not a locked door. It is what lets people borrow freely without fear.

check.q: In the library picture, what is the main purpose of the catalogue, reading passes and sign-in sheet?
opts: They let people use books quickly while keeping them safe
They slow readers down so fewer books are borrowed
They exist so that a committee can reject most requests
They matter only when an outside inspector visits
check.why: Good governance makes use fast and safe at once. The catalogue, passes and records give people confidence to use data, not barriers to stop them.

work: List three places where people wait days for data access and note why.
Ask your team whether they can say who owns each of your top ten tables.
Describe governance to a colleague as an enabler, using one concrete example.

reels.title: Six jobs that get an analyst access by lunch

beats.say: A new analyst starts Monday. How do they get safe access by lunchtime, without anyone emailing a committee?

First, a catalogue lists every table with an owner, a meaning, and a label such as public, internal, or personal. Labels drive everything else. Second, access follows roles. The analyst joins the marketing analyst group and gets read rights on those tables, nothing more.

Third, personal columns are masked by default. A card number shows as stars, then the last four digits. Fourth, lineage records which tables feed which, so a change can be checked before it breaks a dashboard.
Finally, every read is logged, and rows carry a retention date, say seven years, after which they are deleted. Logs are what let you answer who read this customer's data last month.

check.q: Why do data labels such as personal or internal matter so much in governance?
opts: They are the signal that drives access, masking and retention rules
They only make the catalogue look tidy for visitors
They decide how fast queries run on the warehouse
They replace the need for audit logs on reads
check.why: Labels are the shared signal. Access, masking and retention policies key off them, so one tag can protect data everywhere without manual work.

work: Check that your top tables carry a label, an owner and a description.
Replace one named-user grant with a role based group.
Test whether you could list all readers of one customer table last month.

reels.title: Where governance quietly leaks

beats.say: Your masking is switched on, yet an analyst still learned a customer's card number. How?

Masking only hides a column where it is applied. Copy the table into a sandbox, or join on an unmasked ID, and the protection can vanish. Classification has to travel with the data, through lineage, to every copy.
Deletion is the same. A request to erase a customer must reach backups, caches, and derived tables, or the data lives on. Retention jobs need proof that they ran.
And audit logs are only useful if they are complete and kept longer than the data they describe. Otherwise the question of who read it last month has no answer.

check.q: A customer asks to be erased and the main table row is deleted. What is the biggest remaining risk?
opts: Copies in backups, caches and derived tables still hold the data
The catalogue entry for the table will show an old label
Analysts will lose read rights to every other customer
The audit log will refuse to record the deletion
check.why: Erasure must reach every copy. Backups, caches and derived tables are where data survives, which is why lineage is needed to find them.

work: Trace one sensitive column through lineage and list every copy that holds it.
Check that masking rules apply to sandbox and exported copies.
Confirm audit logs are kept longer than the data they cover.

reels.title: Governance by risk, not by default

beats.say: Should every table get full governance on day one? Almost never.

Tag and protect by risk. Cover the few percent of tables holding personal or financial data first, and keep the rest light. Otherwise cost and delay grow, and teams route around you with unofficial copies.

Prefer central policy enforced automatically, such as tags that drive masking, over manual tickets. Tickets do not scale past a few hundred requests a month. But central enforcement needs a platform team, and tool lock in is real.
Judge it by outcomes: hours to grant access, zero raw card numbers exposed, and minutes to answer an audit question.

show.title: Measure outcomes
items: Minutes to answer an audit question

check.q: You have a small team and hundreds of tables. What is the best way to start governance?
opts: Protect the few high risk tables first and automate with tags
Apply full controls to every table before anyone gets access
Wait for a regulator request, then build everything at once
Handle each access request by manual ticket and review
check.why: Risk based rollout gives the most protection for the least effort, and tag driven automation scales where tickets and blanket controls do not.

work: Rank your tables by risk and cover the top tier first.
Pick two outcome metrics, such as hours to access, and track them monthly.
List which governance rules could move from tickets to tag driven policy.

reels.title: Labels on the moving boxes

beats.say: Imagine moving house with a hundred unlabeled boxes. Which one holds your passport?

chip.text: You cannot protect what you cannot find

beats.say: Classification is a label on every item. In data, an item is a column in a table. The label says what is inside: email, phone, card number, or harmless.
Labels matter because they trigger rules. Passport boxes go in the locked car. Kitchen boxes go anywhere. In data, labels decide who can see a column, what gets hidden, and how long it is kept.
Who writes the labels? First the people who packed the box. Then a scanner double checks. Then the owner confirms.

show.title: Who writes the labels
items: The team that made the data

check.q: Why do we label each column as personal or not?
opts: Labels decide which protection rules apply to the column
Labels make the table smaller and faster to query
Labels prove the data is accurate and fully clean
check.why: Tags drive masking, access, retention and audit. Without a label, none of those rules know the column needs protection.

work: List three tables you own and write down which columns would get a personal data label.
Ask which team would be the first to know what a column really holds.

reels.title: Declared, detected, reviewed

beats.say: A column called contact holds ten thousand values. Is it personal data, and who decides?
Layer one is declared. The team producing the data tags columns in the data contract. This is the most reliable source, because they know what each column means.

Layer two is detected. A scanner samples a thousand values and tests patterns: emails, phones, national ids, and card numbers, which must also pass a Luhn check. That is a checksum that rejects random digits.
If ninety percent match email and the threshold is eighty, it proposes pii dot email. Layer three: the owner confirms, and the tag joins the contract.

check.q: A scanner finds 90 percent of sampled values in a column look like emails. What happens next?
opts: The tag is applied at once and never looked at again
A tag is proposed and the owner confirms it into the contract
The column is deleted until a person rewrites its name
check.why: Detection only proposes. The owner reviews, and confirmed tags become part of the contract, so people stay accountable.

work: Check whether your data contracts have a field for column tags, and add one if not.
Pick a landing zone table and run a pattern scan on a sample of 1,000 rows.

reels.title: Where detection slips

beats.say: Why does one email in a free text column not make it an email column?
Detection is statistical. One percent matching fails an eighty percent threshold. So a notes column slips through clean, even though real addresses and phone numbers sit inside it.
Other traps: sampling only the first rows misses later data. A Luhn check passes some order numbers by chance. A name like phone model fools name matching.
False positives cost review time. False negatives leak data. So set the proposal threshold low, and mark free text as unknown, never as clean.

check.q: Why can a free text notes column escape a scanner that has an eighty percent threshold?
opts: Free text columns are exempt from privacy rules by design
Scanners only read column names and never the values
Few values match a pattern, so the rate stays far below the line
check.why: Personal data scattered through free text gives a very low match rate, so a high threshold misses it. Treat such columns as unknown and review them.

work: Find free text columns such as notes or comments and mark them unknown until reviewed.
Sample random rows, not the first rows, when you scan.
Track how many proposals owners reject, to tune the threshold.

reels.title: Scanner as safety net

beats.say: Should you scan every table every night and trust the result?
Scanning costs compute, and sampling reads real personal data. So run scanners inside the secure zone, and scan only new or changed columns, not the whole lake daily.

show.title: Scan smart
items: Not the whole lake each night

beats.say: Declared tags should win. The scanner is a safety net. In landing zones where nobody declared anything, block publishing until each column has a tag or an unknown status.
A tiny estate can tag by hand. A huge one needs a catalog tool. Watch owner rejection rates: if they reject most proposals, they stop reading them, and the process fails.

show.title: Choose by scale
items: Rejection rate shows if reviews still work

check.q: Which design best fits a large data estate?
opts: Declared tags first, with scans on changes as a safety net
Scanner tags only, run over the whole lake every night
Manual tagging only, done once when the table is created
check.why: Producers know the meaning best, so declared tags lead. Targeted scans catch what was missed without wasting compute or over-reading personal data.

work: Add a publishing check that rejects tables with untagged columns.
Move scanning jobs into the secure zone and limit them to changed schemas.
Report the proposal acceptance rate monthly to tune thresholds.

reels.title: The recall trail

beats.say: A bakery finds one bad batch of flour. How do they know which cakes to pull?

show.text: Which cakes used the bad flour?

beats.say: They keep a trail. Every cake records its ingredients, and every ingredient records its batch. Follow the trail forward and you get a list of every affected cake.
Data works the same way. Lineage is a map of which jobs read which tables and write which others. It turns who uses this into a real list instead of a guess.
Labels travel too. If a flour batch is marked allergen, every cake made from it gets the warning automatically. Data tags like personal email do the same.

check.q: What does lineage give a data team that a guess cannot?
opts: A reliable list of what depends on a given table
A faster query engine for large tables
A copy of every table kept for backup
A password for each downstream consumer
check.why: Lineage is a map of which jobs read and write which tables, so who uses this becomes a concrete list. It does not speed queries, back up data or manage passwords.

work: Pick one important table and try to list its consumers from memory, then compare with a lineage view.
Name one label, such as personal email, that should follow data wherever it is copied.

reels.title: How lineage and tags travel

beats.say: A column is tagged personal email. It flows into five tables. How does the tag follow it?
Each job, in Spark, Airflow or dbt, sends an event when it runs. The event lists the tables it read and the tables it wrote. The catalog stitches these events into one graph.
Now ask a question. Rename the email column, and the graph walks downstream: two tables and three dashboards break. That list is the impact.
Tags walk the same edges. The email tag is copied onto every column built from it, so masking and retention rules apply on their own. It stops where a step hashes, aggregates or drops the column.

check.q: A tagged email column feeds a table that only stores a hash of it. What should propagation do?
opts: Stop there, because the hash step removes the raw value
Copy the tag anyway, since the data came from email
Delete the upstream tag to avoid a mismatch
Block the job until someone approves the run
check.why: Propagation follows edges until a step masks, aggregates or drops the data. A hash step is a deliberate end point, so the tag stops there.

work: Check whether your Spark, Airflow and dbt jobs already emit OpenLineage events.
Run an impact query for one column rename and see whether the list matches what you expected.

reels.title: Where lineage lies to you

beats.say: Your lineage graph says nothing uses this column. Can you trust it?
Only if it was captured from the running jobs. Parsing SQL afterwards misses dynamic queries, notebooks and custom functions, so edges silently go missing. A missing edge means a surprise outage.
Tags carry a different risk. Join email with a name and the result is still personal data, but a naive rule might drop the tag. Over tagging is noisy. Under tagging leaks.

show.title: Tag propagation traps
items: Aggregates may be safe, but check

beats.say: Also watch stale edges from jobs that were deleted, and tools that emit no events at all. Show when each edge was last seen, so old paths can expire.

show.title: Keep the graph honest
items: Record last seen time per edge
List tools that emit no events

check.q: Lineage shows no consumers for a column, yet a team uses it in a notebook. What is the likely cause?
opts: The notebook never emitted lineage, so the edge is missing
The column is too old to appear in any graph
Column-level lineage only works for numeric types
The catalog hides edges for tagged columns
check.why: Lineage is only as complete as its sources. Notebooks, custom functions and tools without events leave gaps, so no edges does not mean no users.

work: List the tools in your stack that do not emit lineage events and decide how to cover them.
Add a last seen timestamp to lineage edges and review the oldest ones monthly.

reels.title: How much lineage to buy

beats.say: Should you track column-level lineage for every table? Probably not.

Column detail costs storage, compute and review time, and most tables are never queried by anyone who cares. Keep it for tables with personal data, finance numbers or many consumers. Table level is enough elsewhere.
Prefer emitted OpenLineage events over vendor parsers, so you can switch catalogs. Put the impact check in the pull request, where a warning is cheap, not in an incident review.
And never make propagated tags your only control. Enforce masking at the source with policy, and treat lineage as the way to find gaps. For a small dbt only stack, built in docs may be enough.

show.title: Limits
items: Small stacks may not need a catalog

check.q: What is the best use of column-level lineage in a large estate?
opts: Apply it to sensitive and widely shared tables only
Apply it to every table so nothing is skipped
Replace masking policies with propagated tags
Use it only after an incident to find the cause
check.why: Column detail has real cost, so spend it where risk and consumer count are high. Tags support policy but do not replace it, and the value is highest before incidents, such as in CI.

work: Rank your tables by sensitivity and consumer count, and choose where column lineage is worth it.
Add a pull request check that lists downstream products for any changed column.
Confirm masking is enforced by policy at the source, not only by propagated tags.

reels.title: Shelf life for data

beats.say: Would you keep every receipt you have ever received, forever?

show.sub: Think of a pile of old receipts

beats.say: Probably not. Piles of paper cost space, and someone could read them. Data is the same. A retention policy gives each kind of data a shelf life, like milk lasting days and rice lasting months. When the time is up, the data is thrown out automatically.
Two twists. If a person asks you to forget them, you must search every drawer for their papers. And if a court says keep these papers, you keep them, even past the date. That is called a legal hold.

check.q: A court orders you to keep some papers, but their shelf life has ended. What should happen?
opts: Keep them until the hold is lifted
Delete them because the policy says so
Delete them but keep a short summary
Keep them one more week then delete
check.why: A legal hold overrides retention. The data stays until the hold is formally lifted, whatever the normal expiry date says.

work: List your main data types and write down a shelf life for each one.
Ask legal who can place a hold and how you would be told.
Find one dataset that has no expiry and ask why.

reels.title: Dropping old data, erasing one person

beats.say: How do you delete a year of data without touching a single row?

Retention works on whole partitions. Raw events are kept thirteen months. The table is split by day, so the job just drops each day older than that. No row scanning, so it is cheap. Financial records get seven years, support chat two years, set by tag.

Erasure is harder. One person asks to be forgotten. Lineage and tags tell you every table holding their id. You delete their rows in batches, then compact files and expire old snapshots, because until then the old files still contain them. Backups must follow the same rules.

check.q: Why is dropping day partitions cheaper than erasing one person's data?
opts: Whole files go at once, with no row search
Partitions are encrypted so they delete faster
Erasure needs a manual review for each row
Retention jobs run on bigger machines
check.why: Retention removes whole partitions that aged out. Erasure must find and rewrite rows for one person across many tables.

work: Check that big tables are partitioned by date so retention is a cheap drop.
Map which tables hold a person id using tags and lineage.
Write down the full erasure steps, including backups.

reels.title: Why deleted data comes back

beats.say: You deleted the row. So why can the data still be read?

Table formats like Iceberg keep old snapshots for time travel. A merge-on-read delete only writes a marker saying skip this row. The original file still holds the person's data. Until you compact and expire snapshots, it is recoverable.

chip.text: Compact and expire to truly erase

beats.say: Backups are the next trap. A restore from last month's backup brings the person back. Extracts, caches and training sets hold copies too, so lineage must reach them.
And the legal hold. The deletion job must check holds first. Wrongly deleting held data is worse than keeping extra, because destroying evidence can bring fines.

show.sub: Wrong deletion costs more than extra storage

check.q: After a merge-on-read delete of a person's rows, what is still true until compaction and snapshot expiry?
opts: Old files may still hold the person's data
The data is gone but the marker remains
Only backups still hold the person's data
Queries can still see it but only as admin
check.why: Merge-on-read writes a skip marker. The original files and old snapshots still contain the rows until they are compacted and expired.

work: Test an erasure end to end and try to time travel back to the deleted row.
Schedule compaction and snapshot expiry after erasure batches.
Add backups and downstream copies to your erasure checklist.

reels.title: Designing deletion that scales

beats.say: What does it cost to say yes to every deletion request?

show.sub: Design it in, not on top

beats.say: Design so erasure is cheap. Partition by time for retention. Keep personal details in one small table keyed by person, and let other tables hold only a token. Delete that one row and the rest points at nothing.
Avoid row erasure on huge tables where you can. It rewrites files and burns compute. Batch requests and run them weekly, inside the legal deadline of thirty days.
Keep one hold registry that every deletion job reads, and log every deletion for audit. Fail closed: if the registry is down, delete nothing.

check.q: The hold registry is unreachable when the nightly deletion job starts. What is the safest design?
opts: Skip deletion and alert until it is back
Delete using yesterday's cached hold list
Delete only data older than seven years
Delete everything and restore held data later
check.why: Failing closed is safest. Wrongly deleting held data is irreversible and costly, while a delayed deletion is a small, recoverable cost.

work: Move personal details into one keyed table and use tokens elsewhere.
Build a single hold registry and make every deletion job check it.
Log each deletion with who, what and when for audit.

reels.title: Four ways to hide a person

beats.say: How can a team use customer data without ever seeing who the customers are? There are four different tricks, and people mix them up all the time.

Masking is a black marker over a letter. The words are still on the paper, but the reader only sees stars. Tokenisation is a coat check. You hand over your coat, get a ticket, and only the cloakroom can match ticket to coat.

chip.text: Only the cloakroom can reverse it

beats.say: Pseudonymisation is a nickname. Everyone uses the same nickname, so stories still line up, but a secret list says who you really are. Anonymisation mixes you into a crowd count. Nobody can ever find you again.

chip.text: Only the crowd cannot be traced back

check.q: Which tool lets the same person be recognised across tables but only reveals who they are with a secret?
opts: Pseudonymisation, a consistent stand-in that only a protected key can link back
Masking, because the stars are produced from a secret stored with each row
Anonymisation, because the link to the person is kept in a locked archive
Tokenisation, because each token is a hash that anyone can recompute freely
check.why: Pseudonymisation gives a consistent stand-in so joins work, and only the key links it to a person. Masking only hides display, anonymisation removes the link for good, and tokens are random, not recomputable.

work: Write one sentence for each of the four terms and check your team uses them the same way.
List the columns in your warehouse that hold identifiers and note which tool each one needs.

reels.title: How each technique works

beats.say: A sixteen digit card number. How can four teams each see it a different way?

Masking happens at read time. A policy checks your role, and an analyst sees stars then the last four digits. The stored number never changes. Tokenisation swaps the card for a random token, and only a vault can map it back. A payment service may ask. Analysts cannot.

chip.text: Masking hides the view. Tokens need the vault

beats.say: Pseudonymisation runs the email through a keyed hash. The same email always gives the same output, so orders and support tickets still join. Without the key, nobody can reverse it.
Anonymisation goes further. Report counts by city, and hide any group smaller than ten people. No link back remains.

check.q: Why does a keyed hash of an email still let you join orders to support tickets?
opts: The same email and key always give the same output, so both tables carry a matching value
The hash is reversed during the join, then hidden again before the results are returned
A vault is called on every row of the join to look up the real email for each side
The hash is random per row, and a lookup table lines the two tables up afterwards
check.why: A keyed hash is deterministic: same input and key give the same output, so equal values match across tables. It is not reversed or random, and no vault call is needed.

work: Pick one table with emails and sketch the keyed hash column you would expose instead.
Check which roles see raw card or email values and which see masked ones.

reels.title: The plain hash trap

beats.say: Is a hashed email anonymous? No, and believing it is has caused real privacy breaches.
Emails are guessable. An attacker takes a list of a hundred million known addresses, hashes each one in minutes, and matches them against your column. Every match reveals a person.
The fix is a keyed hash. The secret key lives in a key manager, so guessing alone gets nowhere. But rotating that key changes every output and breaks joins, so plan for it.
And remember the law. Under GDPR, pseudonymised data is still personal data. Only truly anonymised data falls outside it.

show.title: What GDPR says
items: Pseudonymised data is still personal data
Rules on access, retention and deletion still apply
Only truly anonymised data is outside scope

check.q: A teammate says a plain SHA-256 of each email makes the column anonymous. What is wrong?
opts: Attackers can hash lists of known emails and match them, so a keyed hash is needed
SHA-256 is too weak to hash text, so a longer hash such as SHA-512 is required
Hashes can be undone with the original algorithm, so encryption must replace them
Hashed emails break joins across tables, so they cannot serve analytics at all
check.why: Emails are easy to guess, so an unkeyed hash can be matched by hashing a known list. A secret key stops that. The hash length is not the issue, and hashes still join.

work: Find any column built from a plain hash of an email or phone and replace it with a keyed hash.
Document where the hashing key lives, who can read it and how rotation affects joins.

reels.title: When masking and tokens leak

beats.say: If a column is masked, is the value really safe?

Not always. Masking only hides the display. The raw value still sits in storage, so a leaked file or a broad admin role exposes everything. A clever analyst can also filter where email equals a guess, and see whether any rows come back.
Tokenisation has its own gotcha. The vault becomes the crown jewel. If it goes down, every service needing real values stops. If it leaks, the whole mapping is exposed.
So block filters on masked columns, make the vault highly available, and log every detokenise call.

show.title: Close the gaps
items: Block filters and joins on masked columns
Run the vault highly available and backed up
Log every detokenise call for audit

check.q: Why is a masked column not enough to protect an email address by itself?
opts: The raw value stays in storage, and filters or file access can still expose it
Masking encrypts the value with a weak cipher that determined analysts can break
Masking deletes the raw value, so any report that needs it later fails to run
Masking changes the stored value, so downstream joins on that column stop matching
check.why: Masking only changes what a reader sees. The stored value is unchanged, so leaked files, broad roles or filter guessing can still expose it.

work: Test whether an analyst on a masked column can filter or group by the hidden value.
Review vault availability, backups and the audit log of detokenise calls.

reels.title: Choosing the right tool

beats.say: Four tools, one budget. Which do you reach for first?
Default to masking at read time. It is cheap, needs no copies, and follows roles. But the raw data still exists, so it protects views, not storage.

Use tokenisation only where real values must come back, like card numbers. It cuts audit scope, but adds a network call and an outage risk to every payment path. Never detokenise inside analytics queries.
For analysis, pseudonymise in the warehouse. For sharing outside, anonymise, and test it, because small groups can still reveal people.

show.title: Default choices
items: Mask at read for most analysts
Tokenise only when values must be recovered
Anonymise and test before external sharing

check.q: Your analytics team runs heavy queries and needs to join users across ten tables without knowing who they are. What fits best?
opts: Keyed-hash pseudonyms in the warehouse, with the key held by a small trusted group
Tokenise every identifier and call the vault to detokenise inside each analytics query
Mask the id column at read time so every analyst sees stars in place of the value
Anonymise the raw tables by aggregation first, then join the aggregated results
check.why: Keyed pseudonyms are consistent, so joins work at warehouse speed with no vault call. Masked stars cannot join, per-query detokenising is slow and risky, and aggregation removes the row level detail joins need.

work: Write a one page decision guide: which technique for which data and audience.
Measure vault latency and cost before putting tokenisation on a hot path.
Run a re-identification test on any dataset you plan to share outside the company.

reels.title: The sign-in book for data

beats.say: Someone asks who looked at a customer's records last month. Can you answer in a minute, or does it take two weeks?
Think of a building with a sign-in book at the front desk. Each visitor writes a name, a time, a floor, and a reason. Pages are numbered, so nobody can quietly tear one out.
Data needs the same book. An access log records who read which table, when, and why. A grant history records who approved the key. A deletion record shows what you erased.

show.title: Three books
items: Access log: who read what, when, why

beats.say: Auditors do not accept promises. They want the book. Proof beats good intentions, and a good book makes the answer one lookup.

show.sub: The book answers in one lookup

check.q: What does an auditor mainly want to see?
opts: Written proof of who accessed what and when
A policy document saying staff are careful
A verbal promise from the data team lead
A list of tools the company has bought
check.why: Auditors test evidence of what actually happened. Policies and promises state intent, but only records like access logs and grant history prove it.

work: Find out where your warehouse records who read which table today.
Ask who could answer 'who saw this customer?' and how long it would take.
List the three records an auditor would ask you for first.

reels.title: One query: who saw this customer

beats.say: How do you answer, who saw this customer's data last month, with one query?
Step one. Every query engine writes an access log row: user, table, columns, time, tool, and stated purpose. A busy warehouse writes millions of rows a day, so partition the log table by date.
Step two, lineage. The customer lives in a raw table, but also in copies, like a daily mart and a feature table. Lineage lists every downstream table holding that column.
Step three, join. Take the log, filter to the last thirty days, keep tables from lineage, and group by user. Out comes a list of names in seconds.

show.title: The join
show.text: select user, count(*) from access_log a join lineage l on a.table = l.table where l.source = 'raw_customers' and a.day >= today - 30 group by user

check.q: Why is lineage needed to answer who saw this customer's data?
opts: It lists every copy of the data, not just the original
It stores the passwords of each user who read it
It speeds up queries on the raw access log table
It deletes the customer rows from every table
check.why: People read copies such as marts and feature tables. Without lineage you would only find readers of the raw table and miss the rest.

work: Check your access log keeps user, table, columns, time, tool and purpose.
Write the who-saw-this query once and time it on real data.
Confirm lineage covers marts and feature tables, not just raw ones.

reels.title: When the log lies

beats.say: Your access log says nobody touched the table. Why might that still be wrong?

Logs have gaps. A service account shared by ten people hides who really ran the query. Direct reads of files in object storage skip the warehouse log entirely. Cached results never reach the table at all.

show.title: Where gaps hide
items: Shared service accounts hide the real person
Direct file reads bypass the warehouse log
Cached results never touch the table

beats.say: Logs can be altered. Write them to storage that cannot be overwritten, and chain hashes so a missing row shows up. Keep them as long as policy says, often one to seven years.
Deletion is the same trap. Deleting rows is not enough while old snapshots and backups still hold them. Evidence must show tables touched, rows deleted, and snapshots expired.

check.q: A customer erasure request is done. What is the weakest evidence?
opts: Rows deleted in the main table, snapshots untouched
Row counts per table plus snapshot expiry dates
A request ID linked to each table that was cleaned
A dated log of backup expiry for old copies
check.why: Time travel snapshots and backups still hold the erased rows, so the data is recoverable. Real evidence covers every copy, not just the live table.

work: Replace shared service accounts with per-person or per-job identities.
Send logs to write-once storage and set retention to match policy.
Add snapshot expiry to your erasure runbook and record it.

reels.title: What audit evidence costs

beats.say: Should you log every single read, forever? That bill grows fast.
Full column-level logging on a big warehouse can reach terabytes a year. Tier it. Keep ninety days hot for fast queries, then move to a cheap cold archive that is slower to search.

Log more detail for sensitive columns and only summaries for public data. Then measure classification coverage: the share of production columns with a reviewed tag. Without it, you cannot tell which reads matter.

Prefer evidence generated by the platform, like policy in version control and grant records, over spreadsheets and screenshots. Manual evidence goes stale before the audit arrives. Give each report one owner.

show.title: Evidence you trust
items: Policy as code history from version control
Grant and review records from the platform

check.q: What is the best way to control audit log cost?
opts: Tier storage and log more detail for sensitive data
Log only failed queries and drop all successful reads
Keep every log hot so any query stays fast forever
Sample one read in ten to cut volume across tables
check.why: Tiering keeps recent logs fast and old logs cheap, while detail is focused where risk is. Dropping or sampling reads breaks the proof auditors need.

work: Set hot and cold retention tiers for the access log and price them.
Track classification coverage as a number reviewed each month.
Replace one manual evidence spreadsheet with a generated report.

reels.title: Rules that enforce themselves

beats.say: Why does a rule written in a binder never protect anything?
Picture an office building. One way is a binder of rules and a guard who reads it. The other way is doors that check your badge on their own. The binder gets ignored. The doors cannot be.
Data governance as code is the doors. Rules are written as files, checked automatically, and enforced by the platform itself. Marking a column as private, for example, locks it the moment it exists.
And badges expire. Access is granted to a person for a set time, then it switches off, like a visitor pass.

check.q: What makes governance as code different from a rulebook?
opts: The platform enforces the rule automatically, with no one needing to remember it
A larger committee reviews each request more carefully before approval
Staff sign a policy document once a year to confirm they read it
Every dataset is locked until a manager unlocks it by hand
check.why: Code turns a rule into a check or a policy the platform applies every time, so protection does not depend on people remembering a document.

work: Pick one written data rule and find out whether anything actually enforces it.
List who still has access to your most sensitive table and ask why.

reels.title: From a tag to a protected column

beats.say: How does a brand new column get protected before anyone remembers to ask?
A team adds an email column to a data product and tags it personal in the contract. The build runs a check in CI, the automated test step. An untagged column fails the build, so nothing is published.
In the warehouse, a masking policy is attached to the personal tag, not to column names. So the moment that column appears, analysts see hashed values. Only approved roles see the real email.

Access comes through a request. The data owner approves, and the grant expires, say after ninety days. A nightly job deletes rows by tag and class, after checking for legal holds. A dashboard shows coverage.

check.q: Why attach masking policies to tags instead of to named columns?
opts: A new column with the tag is protected immediately, with no extra policy work
Tags make queries run faster because the warehouse can skip masked data
Column names cannot be used inside a warehouse policy at all
Tags let analysts choose which columns they want to see masked
check.why: The policy follows the tag, so any column that carries it is covered the instant it appears, even if nobody updates the policy.

work: Check whether your masking rules are tied to tags or to hard-coded column names.
Add a CI test that fails when a contract column has no classification tag.

reels.title: Deleted, but still there

beats.say: You deleted a customer's rows last night. So why are they still readable?
Table formats keep old snapshots for time travel, so past versions still hold the erased rows. Backups hold copies too. Until those expire, the data is hidden, not gone.

So the erasure job must do more than run a delete. It expires snapshots, compacts files to rewrite them, and follows the backup policy, then records proof. And it checks legal holds first, because a hold beats erasure.
Tags rot in a similar way. Schemas change, and the old tags go stale. Keep tags in contracts, check them in CI, and scan new data to catch a column that looks personal but is untagged.

check.q: An erasure job deletes rows from the live table. What is still missing?
opts: Snapshots, compacted files and backups may still hold the rows until they are handled
Nothing, because a delete statement removes every copy at once
The rows must also be removed from the data contract file
Analysts must be told to clear their query caches by hand
check.why: Time travel snapshots, uncompacted files and backups keep old versions, so true erasure needs snapshot expiry, compaction and a backup policy, plus a hold check first.

work: Find your snapshot retention setting and compare it to your erasure deadline.
Add legal-hold checking and proof logging to your erasure job.

reels.title: Stale grants, role sprawl and shadow copies

beats.say: Why does someone still have access to a project they left three years ago?
Because the grant was made once and never given an end date. Fix it with expiring grants and a quarterly review, where owners confirm or drop each one.

Role explosion is the cousin. Teams make a new role for every odd case until thousands exist and nobody understands them. Keep roles coarse, like analyst or finance. Use tags and attributes for the fine rules.
Shadow copies appear when access is slow. People export to spreadsheets and personal buckets. Make approved access fast, scan storage for strays, and require an owner on every dataset.

check.q: Why do shadow copies in spreadsheets and personal buckets appear?
opts: Approved access is slow or painful, so people work around it
Warehouses cannot export data without a special permission
Masking policies make all data unreadable to analysts
Auditors ask teams to keep local backups of each table
check.why: When the legitimate route is slow, people take the shortcut. Fast, approved access removes the reason, and scanning catches what remains.

work: Report how many grants have no expiry date and set a default end date.
Time how long a typical access request takes, from ask to grant.

reels.title: When governance as code goes wrong

beats.say: When does governance as code make things worse?
When it replaces judgement with rigid gates. Blocking every untagged column stalls delivery if tagging is painful. Give teams templates and suggested tags, so doing the right thing is the easy thing.
Committees fail by taking weeks per request. Move to owners approving, with policy as code setting the limits. Boards only handle new rules and exceptions.

Watch the cost too. Tag-based policies need a good classification tool and a warehouse that supports them. Small teams with a few tables may do better with simple roles and a quarterly review. Measure coverage and time to grant, not document count.

show.title: Choose by scale
items: Few tables: simple roles and reviews
Many products: tags, policy as code
Measure coverage and time to grant

check.q: A small team has ten tables and one analyst group. What fits best?
opts: Simple roles with expiring grants and a periodic review
A full tag-driven policy platform with automated classification
A governance board that reviews every single query
Locking all tables until a formal framework is complete
check.why: Heavy tag-based tooling costs more than it returns at small scale. Simple roles, expiry and review give most of the safety for little effort.

work: Track time to grant and tag coverage as your two headline governance numbers.
Decide which rules need hard gates and which only need a warning and an owner.
